title: Injection Moulding — Cost Drivers
body: Primary cost drivers in order: (1) Mould tool amortisation — dominates at low volumes. (2) Cooling time — proportional to wall thickness squared; reducing wall by 20% cuts cooling by 36%. (3) Clamp force / machine size — larger machine = higher MHR. (4) Material: engineering resins (PA, PC, POM) cost 3–8× commodity PP/PE. (5) Gates and runners — hot runner eliminates regrind and reduces cycle. Break-even vs. alternatives: IM wins above ~5000 parts/year vs. machining.

title: Injection Moulding — Family Indicators
body: Part classified as injection moulded if: uniform thin walls (1–4 mm), draft angles present, ribs and bosses visible, gate vestige or marks, parting line evidence. Complexity increases with: undercuts, inserts, overmoulding, tight tolerances, high-gloss finish requirements.

title: Sheet Metal — Cost Drivers
body: Primary cost drivers: (1) Material — blank area × thickness × density × price/kg. (2) Laser cutting time — proportional to cut length and pierce count, plus speed reduction at corners. (3) Bending — press brake setups are expensive for complex bend sequences; CNC press brake reduces setup time. (4) Welding — adds labour and distortion risk. (5) Coating (powder coat / zinc plate) — area-based. Nest efficiency (material utilisation %) directly drives material cost.

title: CNC Machining — Cost Drivers
body: Primary cost drivers: (1) Setup — fixturing and programming, amortised over batch. (2) Cycle time — driven by material removal rate, surface finish, and feature complexity. (3) Machine type — 5-axis doubles MHR vs. 3-axis but reduces setups for complex parts. (4) Tight tolerances — ±0.01 mm requires additional finishing passes. (5) Material — titanium/Inconel can be 5–10× harder to machine than aluminium. CNC machining is cost-effective for prototypes and low volumes; injection moulding wins above ~5k parts.

title: Die Casting — Cost Drivers
body: Primary cost drivers: (1) Tooling — $30k–$150k for aluminium dies. (2) Machine hourly rate (500T–2500T presses). (3) Cycle time — faster than IM for thin walls (15–60 s). (4) Secondary machining — most die cast parts need CNC finishing. (5) Post-processing: deburring, shot blasting, heat treatment (T6 for structural Al). Break-even vs. IM: die casting wins on thin-wall metal parts above ~10k/year.

title: Additive Manufacturing — When to Use
body: Additive (SLA/SLS/FDM/DMLS) is cost-effective for: prototypes (1–5 parts), complex organic shapes impossible to mould/machine, lattice structures, low-volume end-use (<50 parts). DMLS (metal) has high feedstock cost ($50–$400/kg) and slow build rates; economical only for complex aerospace or medical parts. Not cost-competitive with IM above 100 parts for most geometries.

title: Forging — Design Rules
body: Closed-die forging: draft 5–7°, fillet radii min 3–6 mm, parting line design critical. Flash removed in trimming. Material savings: near-net shape reduces machining. Grain flow follows part contour — better fatigue resistance than machining. Tooling: $20k–$100k. Economic above ~5k parts for structural components.

title: Process Selection — Volume Break-Even Rules of Thumb
body: 1–50 parts: machining or 3D print. 50–2000 parts: machining, vacuum casting, or small-lot IM on aluminium tooling. 2000–10000 parts: injection moulding (steel tool), die casting (zinc). 10000+ parts: IM, die casting, stamping, or forging depending on material and geometry. Always compare (tooling NRE + piece cost × volume) across processes.

title: Sustainability — CO2 Intensity by Process
body: Rough CO2 intensity (kg CO2e per kg of finished part, excluding material): Injection moulding 0.3–0.8, CNC aluminium 3–8, CNC steel 1–4, Die casting aluminium 1.5–3, Sheet metal laser 0.5–1.5, Additive DMLS 8–20. Material production dominates for most parts: virgin aluminium 9–11 kg CO2/kg, recycled aluminium 0.5 kg CO2/kg, virgin PA66 7–9 kg CO2/kg.
